options.B: A train moving on a straight track with constant velocity
options.C: A lift moving upward with constant velocity
options.D: A ship sailing along a straight line at steady speed

correct_answer_text: A car moving along a circular track at constant speed

distractor_rationale.B: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so this frame is inertial.
distractor_rationale.C: Zero acceleration again, so Newton's laws hold in their usual form.
distractor_rationale.D: This frame has no acceleration and is therefore inertial.

solution: A car on a circular track has a centripetal acceleration even though its speed is constant, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing. An accelerated frame is non inertial, so Newton's laws need a pseudo force there. The other three frames move with constant velocity and are inertial.
formula_principle: A frame is inertial if it has zero acceleration. Any accelerated frame, including one turning at constant speed, is non inertial.
common_misconception: Students equate constant speed with zero acceleration and forget that a change of direction is also an acceleration.

concept_tested: Force from a uniform change of velocity
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moving with a velocity of 10 m s^-1 is brought to rest uniformly in 4 s. The magnitude of the retarding force is

distractor_rationale.A: This is the magnitude of the retardation in m s^-2 quoted as though it were the force.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the initial momentum in kg m s^-1, obtained by using m v as the force.
distractor_rationale.D: This comes from dividing the mass by the retardation instead of multiplying.

solution: The retardation is (10 - 0)/4 = 2.5 m s^-2. Hence the force is F = 2 x 2.5 = 5 N, directed opposite to the motion. The same result follows from impulse, since the momentum change is 2 x 10 = 20 kg m s^-1 over 4 s, giving 20/4 = 5 N.
formula_principle: F = m (v - u)/t.
common_misconception: Students report the acceleration or the momentum change as the answer instead of completing the calculation of force.

concept_tested: Third law pair acts on different bodies
stem: A horse pulls a cart forward and the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. The cart nevertheless accelerates forward because

options.A: the force exerted by the horse on the cart is slightly greater than the force exerted by the cart on the horse
options.B: the two forces of the pair act on different bodies, and the net force on the cart alone is forward
options.C: the force exerted by the cart on the horse acts only after a short time delay
options.D: the weight of the cart cancels the backward pull exerted by the cart

correct_answer_text: the two forces of the pair act on different bodies, and the net force on the cart alone is forward

distractor_rationale.A: The third law pair is exactly equal in magnitude at every instant, so nothing is left over.
distractor_rationale.C: Third law forces appear and vanish together with no time lag whatsoever.
distractor_rationale.D: Weight is vertical and cannot cancel a horizontal force.

solution: To find the motion of the cart, only the forces on the cart are collected. These are the forward pull of the horse and the backward friction on the wheels. The backward pull of the cart on the horse appears in the equation of motion of the horse, not of the cart. When the forward pull exceeds the friction on the cart, the cart accelerates.
formula_principle: Third law forces are equal and opposite but act on two different bodies, so they never cancel in the equation of motion of either body.
common_misconception: Students add the action and reaction of a third law pair into one free body diagram and conclude that nothing can ever accelerate.

concept_tested: Apparent weight when the lift accelerates upward
stem: A man of mass 50 kg stands on a weighing machine inside a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the reading of the machine is

distractor_rationale.A: This uses m(g - a), which applies when the acceleration is directed downward.
distractor_rationale.B: This is the true weight, obtained by ignoring the acceleration of the lift.
distractor_rationale.D: This is only the extra term m a, with the weight left out.

solution: The machine reads the normal reaction N. For the man, N - m g = m a with the acceleration upward, so N = m(g + a) = 50 x (10 + 2) = 50 x 12 = 600 N.
formula_principle: For a lift accelerating upward with acceleration a, the normal reaction is N = m(g + a).
common_misconception: Students use m(g - a) whenever the lift is in motion, without checking the direction of the acceleration.

concept_tested: Apparent weight in free fall
stem: The cable of a lift snaps and the lift falls freely. A person of mass 60 kg inside stands on a weighing machine. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the machine reads

distractor_rationale.B: This is the true weight, which is what the machine would read only if the lift were at rest or moving uniformly.
distractor_rationale.C: This comes from adding m g to m a with a taken as g, which corresponds to an upward acceleration of g.
distractor_rationale.D: This corresponds to a downward acceleration of only g/2, not free fall.

solution: In free fall the lift and the person both accelerate downward at g. The equation for the person is m g - N = m g, which gives N = 0. The person and the machine fall together and press on each other with no force, a state described as weightlessness.
formula_principle: N = m(g - a). In free fall a = g, so N = 0.
common_misconception: Students think weightlessness means gravity has disappeared, whereas gravity is precisely what is producing the free fall.

stem: The same constant force acts separately on two bodies X and Y of masses 2 kg and 8 kg, both initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. The ratio of the acceleration of X to that of Y is

concept_tested: Pseudo force in an accelerated frame
stem: Consider two statements. Statement P: Newton's laws in their usual form are valid only in inertial frames. Statement Q: They may still be used in an accelerated frame provided a pseudo force equal in magnitude to the mass times the acceleration of the frame, and opposite to it, is added to every body.

options.A: P is correct and Q is incorrect
options.B: P is incorrect and Q is correct
options.C: Both P and Q are incorrect
options.D: Both P and Q are correct

correct_answer_text: Both P and Q are correct

distractor_rationale.A: The pseudo force device is exactly what makes the laws usable in an accelerated frame.
distractor_rationale.B: Statement P is the standard condition of validity of the laws and is correct.
distractor_rationale.C: Both statements are standard results about frames of reference.

solution: Newton's laws hold in their simple form only in unaccelerated frames. In a frame accelerating with a0, the observed acceleration of a body differs from the true one by a0, and the discrepancy is absorbed by including a pseudo force of magnitude m a0 opposite to a0. Both statements are therefore correct.
formula_principle: In a frame with acceleration a0, add a pseudo force of magnitude m a0 directed opposite to a0 on every body of mass m.
common_misconception: Students believe a pseudo force is a real interaction and try to find its third law partner, which does not exist.

stem: Two perpendicular forces of magnitudes 3 N and 4 N act simultaneously on a body of mass 5 kg lying on a smooth horizontal surface. The magnitude of the acceleration produced is

distractor_rationale.A: This comes from adding the magnitudes as 3 + 4 = 7 N before dividing by the mass.

stem: A man of mass 50 kg stands on a spring balance inside a lift and the balance reads 400 N. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the lift must be

stem: A small bob hangs from the roof of a car by a light string. The car moves along a horizontal road with a constant acceleration of 10 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the string settles at an angle with the vertical of

distractor_rationale.B: This comes from writing sin of the angle as a/(2g) rather than using the correct tangent relation.
distractor_rationale.C: This comes from writing cos of the angle as a/(2g), which is not the correct relation.
distractor_rationale.D: This assumes a horizontal acceleration cannot tilt the string, which contradicts the horizontal equation of motion.

solution: Resolving the tension, the vertical component balances the weight, so T cos of the angle equals m g, and the horizontal component supplies the acceleration, so T sin of the angle equals m a. formula_principle: For a bob hanging in a vehicle with horizontal acceleration a, tan of the angle with the vertical equals a/g.
common_misconception: Students think the string stays vertical because gravity is vertical, forgetting that the bob must also accelerate horizontally.

concept_tested: Identifying a genuine action and reaction pair
stem: A block rests on a horizontal floor. Which of the following is a correct action and reaction pair under the third law?

options.A: The weight of the block and the normal force of the floor on the block
options.B: The weight of the block and the push of the block on the floor
options.C: The push of the floor on the block and the push of the block on the floor
options.D: The weight of the block and the weight of the floor

correct_answer_text: The push of the floor on the block and the push of the block on the floor

distractor_rationale.A: Both of these act on the block itself and are equal only because the block happens to be in equilibrium.
distractor_rationale.B: These act on different bodies but are not partners; they are of different nature and are equal here only by coincidence.
distractor_rationale.D: The weights of two different bodies are unrelated forces exerted by the earth.

solution: The contact interaction between block and floor gives one force on the block from the floor and one force on the floor from the block. These form the pair. The weight of the block is gravitational and its partner is the pull of the block on the earth. Weight and normal reaction act on the same body and so can never be a third law pair, even though they are numerically equal when the block is in equilibrium on a horizontal floor.
formula_principle: A third law pair is equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, of the same nature, and consists of one force on each of the two interacting bodies.
common_misconception: Students treat any two equal and opposite forces as an action and reaction pair without checking that they act on different bodies.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration set by a breaking tension
stem: A monkey of mass 20 kg climbs a rope that can withstand a maximum tension of 300 N. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the greatest upward acceleration with which the monkey can climb without breaking the rope is

distractor_rationale.A: This comes from writing the limiting condition as T = m a and leaving out the weight.
distractor_rationale.C: This comes from writing the condition as T = m(a - g), which reverses the role of gravity.
distractor_rationale.D: This simply sets the acceleration equal to g without using the strength of the rope.

solution: The rope tension must satisfy T = m(g + a) and cannot exceed 300 N. Hence 20(10 + a) is at most 300, so 10 + a is at most 15 and a is at most 5 m s^-2. If the monkey merely hangs on, the tension is 200 N, and if it climbs with acceleration 5 m s^-2 the tension reaches exactly 300 N.
formula_principle: For a body climbing with upward acceleration a, T - m g = m a, so T = m(g + a).

concept_tested: Statement of the impulse momentum theorem
stem: The impulse of a force acting on a body during a time interval is equal to

options.A: the change in the kinetic energy of the body
options.B: the linear momentum of the body at the end of the interval
options.C: the rate of change of momentum of the body

subtopic: Force from rate of change of momentum
concept_tested: Why a fielder pulls his hands back
stem: A fielder draws his hands backward while catching a fast moving ball. This action

options.A: reduces the impulse received by the hands so that the force becomes smaller
options.B: reduces the momentum of the ball before it reaches the hands
options.C: increases the impulse but spreads it over a larger area of the palm
options.D: increases the time of impact so that the average force on the hands is reduced, the impulse being the same

correct_answer_text: increases the time of impact so that the average force on the hands is reduced, the impulse being the same

distractor_rationale.A: The impulse is fixed by the momentum the ball must lose and cannot be altered by the fielder.
distractor_rationale.B: The ball already carries its momentum, and moving the hands cannot remove it in advance.
distractor_rationale.C: Spreading over an area changes the pressure, not the impulse or the average force.

solution: The ball must lose all its momentum, so the impulse delivered is fixed at m v whatever the fielder does. distractor_rationale.A: Placing gamma in the denominator would make the corrected speed smaller than Newton's value, whereas it must be larger.
distractor_rationale.B: The factor gamma must appear under the square root, since it multiplies the bulk modulus and not the speed.
distractor_rationale.C: This inverts the ratio and would give an answer with the wrong dimensions for a speed.

solution: Laplace pointed out that the compressions and rarefactions succeed each other far too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, so each element behaves adiabatically. The adiabatic bulk modulus of an ideal gas is gamma P instead of P, and inserting this into v = sqrt(E / rho) gives v = sqrt(gamma P / rho). For air with gamma = 1.4 this raises Newton's value by a factor sqrt(1.4), bringing it into agreement with experiment.
formula_principle: Adiabatic bulk modulus of a gas is gamma P, so v = sqrt(gamma P / rho).
common_misconception: Writing gamma outside the square root or in the denominator.

concept_tested: Ordering the speed of sound in the three states of matter
stem: For most ordinary materials, the speed of sound is

options.A: greatest in gases, smaller in liquids and least in solids
options.B: greatest in liquids, smaller in gases and least in solids
options.C: the same in all three states, being fixed only by the temperature
options.D: greatest in solids, smaller in liquids and least in gases

correct_answer_text: greatest in solids, smaller in liquids and least in gases

distractor_rationale.A: This reverses the true order; the very high elasticity of a solid makes sound travel fastest through it.
distractor_rationale.B: Sound in a liquid is faster than in a gas but slower than in a typical solid.
distractor_rationale.C: Temperature matters within one medium, but the elastic modulus differs enormously between the three states.

solution: Going from a gas to a liquid to a solid, the density rises by a factor of roughly a thousand, but the relevant elastic modulus rises by a factor of about a million. common_misconception: Reasoning only from density and concluding that the heaviest medium must be the slowest.

concept_tested: Physical reason for the failure of the isothermal assumption
stem: Newton's isothermal assumption fails for sound in air because

options.A: air is such a good conductor of heat that the temperature can never be held constant during a compression
options.B: the pressure of the atmosphere is far too small for the isothermal bulk modulus to be meaningful
options.C: the compressions and rarefactions follow one another too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, and air is in any case a poor conductor
options.D: sound waves in air are transverse rather than longitudinal, so no compression takes place

correct_answer_text: the compressions and rarefactions follow one another too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, and air is in any case a poor conductor

distractor_rationale.A: It is the poor conductivity of air, not a high conductivity, that keeps each element thermally isolated.
distractor_rationale.B: The magnitude of the pressure is not the issue; the same pressure appears in the corrected formula as well.
distractor_rationale.D: Sound in air is longitudinal and does compress the medium; that is the very mechanism of propagation.

solution: For an audible note there are hundreds or thousands of compressions per second, so each region is squeezed and released in a fraction of a millisecond. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so in that short time almost no heat can flow from a warm compression to a cool rarefaction. formula_principle: Rapid alternation plus the low thermal conductivity of air make the changes adiabatic rather than isothermal.
common_misconception: Believing that the failure is caused by air conducting heat too well rather than too poorly.

concept_tested: Verifying that sqrt(P / rho) has the dimensions of speed
stem: The dimensions of the quantity sqrt(P / rho), where P is a pressure and rho is a density, are

distractor_rationale.A: This is the dimension of an acceleration and would follow only if the square root were omitted from a different combination.
distractor_rationale.B: This is the dimension of pressure itself, before dividing by the density and taking a square root.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the dimension of P / rho before the square root is taken.

solution: Pressure is force per area, so [P] = M L T^-2 / L^2 = M L^-1 T^-2. Density is mass per volume, so [rho] = M L^-3. Dividing, [P / rho] = M L^-1 T^-2 / M L^-3 = L^2 T^-2, which is the square of a speed. Taking the square root gives L T^-1, confirming that both Newton's formula and Laplace's corrected form are dimensionally sound. Note that gamma is a pure number and does not affect the dimensions.
formula_principle: [P] = M L^-1 T^-2 and [rho] = M L^-3, so [P / rho] = L^2 T^-2 and its square root is L T^-1.
common_misconception: Stopping at L^2 T^-2 and forgetting that the square root has still to be taken.

concept_tested: Identifying which quantities affect the speed of sound in a gas
stem: Four quantities are listed for a sample of air. P: the temperature. Q: the pressure at constant temperature. R: the humidity. S: the loudness of the sound. The quantities that affect the speed of sound in the air are

distractor_rationale.A: Pressure has no effect at constant temperature, since rho changes with P so that P / rho stays fixed.
distractor_rationale.B: The inclusion of pressure is wrong, because its effect is exactly cancelled by the accompanying change of density.
distractor_rationale.C: Loudness is set by amplitude, which does not appear anywhere in v = sqrt(gamma P / rho).

solution: Temperature raises the speed as the square root of the absolute temperature, so P is correct. A change of pressure at constant temperature changes rho in exactly the same proportion, leaving P / rho and hence v unaltered, so Q is wrong. Humidity replaces heavier nitrogen and oxygen molecules by lighter water molecules, lowering rho and raising the speed, so R is correct. Loudness is a matter of amplitude and does not enter the formula at all, so S is wrong.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) = sqrt(gamma R T / M): only temperature and composition matter.
common_misconception: Reading the symbol P in the formula as evidence that raising the pressure must raise the speed.

stem: Two diatomic gases X and Y have the same value of gamma, and the molar mass of Y is four times that of X. Gas X is at 300 K. The temperature at which the speed of sound in Y equals that in X is

distractor_rationale.A: Doubling the absolute temperature raises the speed only by sqrt(2), which does not make up a factor of two.
distractor_rationale.B: At the same temperature the heavier gas carries sound at half the speed, so the two cannot match.
distractor_rationale.D: Lowering the temperature of the heavier gas makes its sound speed smaller still, widening the gap.

stem: The sensation of a sound persists in the human ear for about 0.1 s. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the minimum distance of a reflecting wall from a listener if a distinct echo is to be heard is

concept_tested: Behaviour of a compression reflected from a denser medium
stem: A compression pulse travelling through air is incident normally on a rigid wall. The reflected pulse is

options.A: a rarefaction, and the displacement of the particles suffers no phase change on reflection
options.B: a compression, and neither the pressure nor the displacement suffers any phase change

distractor_rationale.B: The displacement must reverse at a rigid wall, since the wall cannot move.

options.B: the field is zero and the potential falls steadily towards the centre
options.C: both the field and the potential have their maximum values at the centre
options.D: the field is zero and the potential equals the potential at the surface

correct_answer_text: the field is zero and the potential equals the potential at the surface

distractor_rationale.A: A zero potential inside would require work to be done in moving a charge from the surface inwards, but no field acts there to require such work.
distractor_rationale.B: A falling potential implies a non zero field, since the field is the rate of fall of potential with distance.
distractor_rationale.C: The field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero everywhere, so it cannot peak at the centre.

solution: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside the conducting material and in the hollow is zero. Since the field measures how fast the potential changes with distance, a zero field means the potential does not change. So the potential everywhere inside equals its value on the surface, which is k q / R for a sphere of radius R.
formula_principle: E = 0 inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, so V is constant throughout it

stem: Two silicon samples are doped to the same majority carrier concentration, one with phosphorus and the other with boron. At the same temperature

options.B: the phosphorus doped sample has the higher conductivity, because electron mobility exceeds hole mobility
options.C: both samples have exactly the same conductivity, because the carrier concentrations are equal

correct_answer_text: the phosphorus doped sample has the higher conductivity, because electron mobility exceeds hole mobility

distractor_rationale.A: The mobilities are the wrong way round; holes move by successive bound electron jumps and are the slower carriers.
distractor_rationale.C: Conductivity is the product of concentration and mobility, and the two mobilities differ.
distractor_rationale.D: Doping with boron suppresses the electron population through the mass action law rather than preserving it.

With the same majority concentration the conductivities are in the ratio of the mobilities, and since mu_e exceeds mu_h the n type sample conducts better.

stem: According to Wien's displacement law, the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly and its absolute temperature are related so that

options.A: the wavelength increases as the temperature increases, their ratio being a constant
options.B: the wavelength is independent of the temperature
options.C: the wavelength decreases as the temperature increases, their product being a constant
options.D: the wavelength is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature

correct_answer_text: the wavelength decreases as the temperature increases, their product being a constant

distractor_rationale.A: Reverses the relation, so a hotter body would glow redder rather than bluer
distractor_rationale.B: Removes the temperature dependence, which would mean every hot body glows with the same colour
distractor_rationale.D: Borrows the fourth power of Stefan's law, which governs the total energy and not the peak wavelength

solution: Wien's law states lambda_max T = b, a constant. The peak of the emission curve therefore shifts towards shorter wavelengths as the temperature rises, which is why a heated body glows first dull red, then orange and finally bluish white.
formula_principle: lambda_max x T = b, with b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K
common_misconception: Learners think a hotter body must emit longer wavelengths because it emits more energy.

concept_tested: Expression for net loss of energy by a body in surroundings
stem: A black body at absolute temperature T is placed in surroundings at absolute temperature T0, where T is greater than T0. The net energy lost by the body per unit time per unit area is

distractor_rationale.B: Raises the temperature difference to the fourth power instead of subtracting the fourth powers
distractor_rationale.C: Adds the two terms, which would make a body in hot surroundings lose energy faster than in cold ones
distractor_rationale.D: Uses a linear difference, which is the approximate form valid only for very small temperature differences

solution: The body radiates sigma T^4 per unit area per unit time and simultaneously absorbs sigma T0^4 from its surroundings. The net loss is the difference, sigma (T^4 - T0^4). formula_principle: Net rate of loss per unit area = sigma (T^4 - T0^4)

concept_tested: Statement and range of validity
stem: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat by a body is proportional to the excess of its temperature over that of the surroundings. This law is

options.A: valid for any temperature difference however large
options.B: valid only when the excess of temperature over the surroundings is small
options.C: valid only when the body is a perfectly black body
options.D: valid only when the surroundings are at absolute zero

correct_answer_text: valid only when the excess of temperature over the surroundings is small

distractor_rationale.A: Ignores that the law is an approximation to the fourth power law and fails when the difference is large
distractor_rationale.C: Adds a condition on the surface that the law does not require; the law applies to any body cooling under a small excess temperature
distractor_rationale.D: Reverses the requirement; if the surroundings were at absolute zero the excess of temperature would be enormous

solution: Newton's law of cooling is an approximation of Stefan's law. If T = T0 + dT with dT small compared with T0, then T^4 - T0^4 is nearly 4 T0^3 dT, which is proportional to the excess temperature. The approximation therefore holds only while the excess is small, and it also requires that the surroundings stay at a steady temperature and that the loss is not dominated by forced convection.
formula_principle: For small excess temperature, sigma (T^4 - T0^4) reduces to a term proportional to (T - T0)
common_misconception: Learners treat Newton's law of cooling as exact for all temperature differences.

stem: As a metal block is heated to higher and higher temperatures, the colour of the light it emits changes from dull red to bluish white. This happens because

concept_tested: Two stage cooling problem
stem: A body cools from 60 degree celsius to 50 degree celsius in 5 minutes in surroundings at 20 degree celsius. Assuming Newton's law of cooling, the time it takes to cool from 50 degree celsius to 40 degree celsius is

distractor_rationale.A: Assumes equal temperature drops always take equal times, which would be true only if the rate of cooling did not change
distractor_rationale.C: Uses the ratio of excess temperatures the wrong way round, making the cooler body cool faster
distractor_rationale.D: Uses the initial and final temperatures rather than the mean temperature of each stage

solution: In the first stage the mean temperature is (60 + 50) / 2 = 55, so the excess over the surroundings is 35. The rate is 10 / 5 = 2 degree per minute, giving 2 = 35 k, so k = 2/35. In the second stage the mean temperature is (50 + 40) / 2 = 45 and the excess is 25. The rate is 25 k = 25 x 2 / 35 = 10/7 degree per minute, so the time for a 10 degree fall is 10 divided by 10/7 = 7 minutes.
formula_principle: Rate of cooling = k x (mean temperature of the body minus temperature of surroundings)
common_misconception: Learners use the instantaneous temperatures instead of the mean temperature of each stage, or assume equal drops take equal times.

stem: A solid sphere behaves as a black body. Its radius is doubled while its absolute temperature is reduced to half. The total power radiated by the sphere becomes

concept_tested: Showing that the fourth power law reduces to a linear law
stem: A body at absolute temperature T is placed in surroundings at absolute temperature T0, with the excess T minus T0 very small compared with T0. Under this condition the net rate of loss of energy per unit area, sigma (T^4 - T0^4), reduces to a form proportional to

options.A: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving sigma T0
options.B: (T - T0)^4, the constant of proportionality being sigma
options.C: (T^2 - T0^2), the constant of proportionality involving 2 sigma T0
options.D: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving 4 sigma T0^3

correct_answer_text: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving 4 sigma T0^3

distractor_rationale.A: Gets the linear dependence right but loses the factor 4 T0^3 that comes from expanding the fourth power
distractor_rationale.B: Replaces the difference of fourth powers by the fourth power of the difference, which is not a valid step
distractor_rationale.C: Stops after factorising only once and keeps a quadratic difference instead of reducing to a linear one

solution: Write T = T0 + dT. Then T^4 - T0^4 = (T^2 - T0^2)(T^2 + T0^2) = (T - T0)(T + T0)(T^2 + T0^2). For a small excess, T is nearly T0, so (T + T0) is nearly 2 T0 and (T^2 + T0^2) is nearly 2 T0^2. The product becomes (T - T0) x 2 T0 x 2 T0^2 = 4 T0^3 (T - T0). Hence the net rate of loss is nearly 4 sigma T0^3 (T - T0), which is directly proportional to the excess of temperature. This is exactly Newton's law of cooling, and it shows why that law holds only for a small excess temperature.
formula_principle: sigma (T^4 - T0^4) is approximately 4 sigma T0^3 (T - T0) when T - T0 is small
common_misconception: Learners try to obtain the linear law by simply replacing the difference of fourth powers with the fourth power of the difference.

concept_tested: Zeroth law of thermodynamics
stem: Which statement is the zeroth law of thermodynamics?

options.A: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
options.B: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, heat flows from the hotter of the two to the colder one.
options.C: The heat supplied to a system equals the rise in its internal energy plus the work done by the system.
options.D: Heat cannot flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter body.

correct_answer_text: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

distractor_rationale.B: This adds a spurious heat flow. The zeroth law asserts equilibrium between the first two systems, which means exactly that no heat flows between them.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the statement of the first law of thermodynamics, which is about energy conservation and not about the definition of temperature.
distractor_rationale.D: This is the Clausius form of the second law, which fixes the direction of spontaneous heat flow rather than establishing thermal equilibrium as transitive.

solution: The zeroth law states that if system X is in thermal equilibrium with system Z, and system Y is also in thermal equilibrium with Z, then X and Y are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This transitivity is what allows a single number, the temperature, to be attached to every system.
formula_principle: Zeroth law: thermal equilibrium is a transitive relation, which allows temperature to be defined.
common_misconception: Students confuse the zeroth law with the first or the second law because all three are stated in similar language.

stem: Two bodies in thermal contact are found to be in thermal equilibrium. Which quantity is necessarily the same for the two bodies?

options.A: internal energy, as a function of the state of a system alone

concept_tested: Temperature, not stored energy, drives heat flow
stem: Block X of mass 2 kg and block Y of mass 1 kg are made of the same metal. X is at 300 K and Y is at 320 K. They are brought into thermal contact and isolated from the surroundings. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Heat flows from X to Y, because X holds the larger internal energy.
options.B: No heat flows, because the products of mass and temperature are nearly equal for the two blocks.
options.C: Heat flows from Y to X, even though X may hold the larger internal energy.
options.D: Heat flows from Y to X until the two blocks hold equal internal energies.

correct_answer_text: Heat flows from Y to X, even though X may hold the larger internal energy.

distractor_rationale.A: Direction of heat flow is decided by temperature alone; the larger store of energy in X is irrelevant.
distractor_rationale.B: The product of mass and temperature has no physical significance in deciding equilibrium; only equality of temperature matters.
distractor_rationale.D: The flow stops when the temperatures become equal, and at that stage the heavier block still holds more internal energy.

solution: Y is at the higher temperature of 320 K, so heat flows from Y to X. For the same metal, internal energy is proportional to mass times temperature, so X with 2 kg at 300 K holds more energy than Y with 1 kg at 320 K, yet it still receives heat. Flow stops when both reach a common temperature between 300 K and 320 K.
formula_principle: Heat flows from higher to lower temperature; equilibrium is equality of temperature, not of internal energy.

stem: Which of the following describes the relation between the electric field and the electric potential correctly?

correct_answer_text: The field can be zero where the potential is not zero, and the potential can be zero where the field is not zero

distractor_rationale.A: Overlooks that a constant non zero potential also gives a zero field.
distractor_rationale.C: Overlooks the equatorial point of a dipole, where the potential vanishes but the field does not.

stem: The occurrence of a small number of alpha particles scattered through very large angles was taken by Rutherford as evidence that

options.A: the electrons inside the atom are arranged in fixed circular shells
options.B: the atom contains an equal number of positive and negative charges
options.C: the positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small volume

distractor_rationale.A: Shell structure was introduced later by Bohr to explain spectra; the scattering data say nothing about how the electrons are arranged.
distractor_rationale.B: Electrical neutrality was already known from ordinary chemistry and is not what the large angle events reveal.

solution: To turn an energetic alpha particle through more than 90 degrees the repulsive Coulomb force must be enormous, which is possible only if the alpha particle can approach very close to a large positive charge. In a uniformly spread positive charge the field inside falls towards zero at the centre and no such force arises. options.A: largest, so that the alpha particle spends the longest time near the nucleus
options.B: smallest, tending to zero for a head on collision
options.C: equal to the nuclear radius, so that the alpha particle grazes the nuclear surface

stem: The number of alpha particles scattered per unit time into a given small angular range about a scattering angle theta is proportional to 1/(sin(theta/2))^4. The ratio of the number scattered at 60 degrees to the number scattered at 120 degrees is

stem: A full wave rectifier working from a 50 Hz mains has a capacitor filter across its load. If the load resistance is increased, the ripple in the output

stem: A Zener diode has a sharp and well defined breakdown voltage because

options.A: both its regions are very lightly doped, giving a wide depletion layer

concept_tested: Distinction between Zener and avalanche breakdown
stem: Zener breakdown differs from avalanche breakdown in that Zener breakdown

options.A: occurs in lightly doped junctions at high reverse voltages through collisions that multiply carriers
options.B: occurs only when the junction is forward biased
options.C: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds
options.D: permanently destroys the junction every time it happens

correct_answer_text: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds

distractor_rationale.A: Describes avalanche breakdown, which is the other mechanism.
distractor_rationale.B: Both breakdown mechanisms belong to the reverse biased condition.
distractor_rationale.D: Breakdown is fully reversible so long as the current is limited by an external resistance.

solution: In a heavily doped junction the depletion layer is very thin, so a reverse voltage of only a few volt produces an enormous field that tears electrons directly out of covalent bonds. That is Zener breakdown. In a lightly doped junction the layer is wide, the field is smaller, and breakdown occurs only at a higher voltage when carriers gain enough kinetic energy between collisions to create new pairs. That is avalanche breakdown.
formula_principle: Zener breakdown is field ionisation in a very thin heavily doped junction; avalanche breakdown is carrier multiplication by collision in a wider junction.
common_misconception: The two mechanisms are treated as one; they differ in doping, in breakdown voltage and in physical cause.
